latin.443: Pergis & ducis argumentum a sententia, quam Deus Adamo prolapso in peccatum pronunciavit his verbis, quia paruisti voci uxoris tuae, & comedisti ex arbore &c. Inde sic argumentaris, Si poena fuit communis, peccatum debuit etiam esse commune. Atqui poena fuit communis. Ergo etiam peccatum. Majorem probas hoc syllogismo, Justus Judex non infligit poenam communem omnibus hominibus, nisi ob commune peccatum omnium. Subit animum tuum hoc totum posse a me concedi, qui agnosco peccatum commune omnium hominum, nempe vitium haereditarium dignum communibus poenis.
latin.444: Itaque longius proveheris. Jam, inquis, assumo, primum illud peccatum quod omnes homines addixit poenae commune est omnibus, vel actu proprio, vel imputatione: Non actu proprio, quia solus Adamus actu peccavit. Ergo imputatione, quia scilicet omnibus imputatur. Cur tertium membrum omisisti tantopere adversus Pelagianos decantatum, vel propagatione naturali? Constat enim primum peccatum in nos transiisse (non qua fuit actio transiens, sed qua fuit aversio a Deo & conversio ad creaturas ut ad finem ultimum, permanens in Adamo) transiisse inquam non imputatione quae extra nos est, sed vera communicatione & propagatione.
latin.445: Ob hoc peccatum commune omnium communes irrogantur omnibus poenae: non satisfactoriae quidem illae in hac vita, saltem respectu fidelium, sed tamen poenae: Irrogatur etiam, nisi gratia Christi intercedat, poena satisfactoria, sed quae nunquam satisfactionem absolvit, mors aeterna. Ego igitur inter actum primi peccati & imputationem interpono in omnibus Adami posteris corruptionem haereditariam quae imputetur nobis ad illas poenas.
latin.446: Cur tam longe quaeris causam proximam malorum quae omnes patimur, cum occurrat in proximo? Cur eam quaeris in Adamo cum in nobis singulis se prodat? Cur opus est ut Deus nobis imputet peccatum alienum, cum in nobis inveniat peccatum quod illas poenas meretur? Cur imputet actuale quod neque actu neque potentia fecimus, cum videat in singulis nobis vitium actu inhaerens dignum illis poenis?
latin.447: Repones fortasse miserias huius vitae & mortem corporis inflictas fuisse Adamo ob peccatum actuale, quia, inquit Deus, paruisti voci uxoris tuae & comedisti ex arbore quam praecepi tibi dicendo &c. Et sic colliges, cujus peccati poenas luimus, id peccatum nostrum est. Peccati actualis Adami poenas luimus. Nostrum est igitur; quomodo, nisi imputatione? Quid si concedam (quod feci in constituendo statu quaestionis) nobis peccatum Adami imputari ac nostrum esse, sed mediate tantum; quia illi participatione vitiositatis, quam in Adamo reliquit, communicamus, & habituali voluntatis pravitate ab eo derivata ei consentimus? Tria enim ista sese ordine consequuntur, peccatum actuale Adami, corruptio nobis inhaerens, poena. Haec nascitur proxime a corruptione nobis inhaerente, corruptio a peccato actuali Adami. Relege, si placet, verba Aegidii Hunnii, quae Cap. 2. dum statum quaestionis constituerem, adscripsi, necnon Chamieri, quorum locum ibidem notavi.
latin.448: Formaliter etiam ad praemissas respondeo hac distinctione, Cujus peccati poenas luimus proxime, seu immediate, Id peccatum nostrum est. Concedo. Cujus vero peccati poenas luimus tantum mediate, alio scilicet mediante peccato, id peccatum nostrum est, Nego. Satis enim est, si sit causa nostri peccati. Nosti enim tritum illud in scholis, quod est causa causae, id etiam est causa causati. Atqui peccati actualis poenas luimus proxime, Nego; Mediate, Concedo. Est igitur nostrum peccatum, non sequitur; sed bene, est causa peccati nostri.

pass_a.443: Next the opponent draws from the sentence God pronounced on fallen Adam—'because you obeyed your wife's voice and ate from the tree…': if the penalty was common, the sin ought also to have been common; but the penalty was common; therefore the sin too. He proves the major: a just Judge does not inflict a common penalty on all men except for a sin common to all. Placeus notes the whole can be granted by him who acknowledges a common sin of all—namely hereditary vice worthy of common penalties.
pass_a.444: The opponent then lengthens the chain: that first sin which doomed all is common either by each one's own deed or by imputation; not by own deed—Adam alone actually sinned—so by imputation to all. Why drop the third limb so often rung against Pelagians: natural propagation? The first sin crossed into us not as a fleeting act but as lasting aversion from God and turn to creatures as last end in Adam—and it crossed not by an imputation standing outside us, but by real sharing and propagation.
pass_a.445: On account of that shared sin, shared penalties fall on all—not fully satisfactory in this life for the faithful, yet still penalties—and without Christ's grace there falls also a satisfactory penalty that never completes satisfaction: eternal death. Between the first sin's act and imputation Placeus therefore sets, in all Adam's seed, hereditary corruption imputed to us for those penalties.
pass_a.446: Why hunt so far for the near cause of evils we all bear, when it stands next to you? Why look for it in Adam when each of us displays it? Why must God charge us with another's sin when he already finds in us a sin that earns those pains? Why charge an actual deed we never did in act or power, while he sees in each a vice now sticking in us and deserving those pains?
pass_a.447: Perhaps you reply that this life's miseries and bodily death were inflicted on Adam for actual sin, because God said 'you obeyed your wife's voice and ate…'—and so you gather: whose sin's penalties we pay, that sin is ours; we pay Adam's actual sin's penalties; therefore it is ours—how, unless by imputation? What if Placeus grants (as in setting the status of the question) that Adam's sin is imputed to us and is ours, but only mediately—because by sharing the viciousness he left in Adam we communicate with him, and by habitual will-depravity derived from him we consent to him? These three follow in order: Adam's actual sin, corruption inhering in us, penalty. The penalty is born proximately from the corruption in us; the corruption from Adam's actual sin. Reread Hunnius and Chamier as cited in Cap. 2 when the status was set.
pass_a.448: To the premises Placeus also answers by a formal cut: if we pay a sin's penalties near at hand—immediately—then that sin is ours: granted. If we pay them only through another intervening sin—mediately—then calling that remote sin 'ours' is denied. Being cause of our sin is enough. The school tag holds: cause of the cause is cause of the effect. That we pay Adam's actual-sin penalties immediately—denied; mediately—granted. So 'therefore it is our sin' does not follow; what follows is that it causes our sin. Tip before the sentence's personal address ('you obeyed your wife's voice…').

443: You go on and draw an argument from the sentence which God pronounced to Adam fallen into sin in these words, because you obeyed your wife's voice, and ate from the tree, and so on. From there you argue thus: If the penalty was common, the sin ought also to have been common. But the penalty was common. Therefore the sin also. You prove the major by this syllogism: A just Judge does not inflict a common penalty on all men except for a sin common to all. It occurs to your mind that this whole can be conceded by me, who acknowledge a sin common to all men, namely hereditary vice worthy of common penalties.
444: So you press further. Now, you say, I assume that first sin which sentenced all men to penalty is common to all, either by their own act, or by imputation: Not by their own act, because Adam alone actually sinned. Therefore by imputation, because namely it is imputed to all. Why did you omit the third member so greatly sung against the Pelagians—or by natural propagation? For it is established that the first sin passed into us (not as it was a transient action, but as it was aversion from God and conversion to creatures as to the ultimate end, remaining in Adam)—passed, I say, not by an imputation which is outside us, but by true communication and propagation.
445: For this sin common to all, common penalties are inflicted on all: not indeed satisfactory ones in this life, at least with respect to the faithful, but penalties nonetheless: There is inflicted also, unless the grace of Christ intervene, a satisfactory penalty, but one which never finishes satisfaction—eternal death. I therefore between the act of the first sin and imputation interpose in all Adam's posterity hereditary corruption which is imputed to us unto those penalties.
446: Why do you seek so far the proximate cause of the evils which we all suffer, when it meets you near at hand? Why do you seek it in Adam when in each of us it shows itself? Why is it needful that God impute to us an alien sin, when in us he finds a sin which merits those penalties? Why should he impute an actual sin which we did neither in act nor in potency, when he sees in each of us a vice actually inhering, worthy of those penalties?
447: You will perhaps reply that the miseries of this life and the death of the body were inflicted on Adam for actual sin, because, God says, you obeyed your wife's voice and ate from the tree which I commanded you, saying, and so on. And so you will gather: whose sin's penalties we pay, that sin is ours. We pay the penalties of Adam's actual sin. It is ours, therefore; how, unless by imputation? What if I concede (as I did in constituting the status of the question) that Adam's sin is imputed to us and is ours, but only mediately; because by participation in the viciousness which he left in Adam we communicate with him, and by the habitual depravity of will derived from him we consent to him? For these three follow one another in order: Adam's actual sin, the corruption inhering in us, the penalty. This is born proximately from the corruption inhering in us; the corruption from Adam's actual sin. Reread, if you please, the words of Aegidius Hunnius which I wrote down in Cap. 2 while constituting the status of the question, and also of Chamier, whose place I noted there.
448: Formally also I answer the premises by this distinction: Whose sin's penalties we pay proximately, or immediately—That sin is ours. I concede. But whose sin's penalties we pay only mediately, another sin namely intervening—that sin is ours: I deny. For it is enough if it is the cause of our sin. For you know that worn saying in the schools: what is the cause of the cause is also the cause of the caused. But that we pay the penalties of the actual sin proximately—I deny; Mediately—I concede. Therefore it is our sin does not follow; but well, it is the cause of our sin.
